Let’s talk about something we all wrestle with, even if we don’t always see it— letting go of the need to be right.
You know that feeling when you’re absolutely sure you have the facts, or you just know you’re standing on the moral high ground? There’s a certain comfort there, isn’t there? It feels safe—sometimes even powerful. But here’s the thing: when we get stuck on being right, we start building invisible walls. Conversations can turn into competitions, and before we know it, relationships start feeling like battlegrounds.
Think about a family dinner—maybe you’ve been there—where two siblings get into a heated debate about politics. Voices get louder, faces turn red, and suddenly, everyone else at the table goes quiet, just watching the tension rise. One sibling, feeling totally misunderstood, storms off down the hall. The other sits there, arms folded, convinced they’ve “won” the argument. But as the night goes on, that victory? It starts to feel pretty empty. Then, later, there’s a quiet knock at the door—a simple, “I’m sorry.” No more arguments, just a moment of real connection. And suddenly, it’s clear—being right isn’t as important as being together.
We all fall into this trap. We defend our positions, sometimes without even realizing it, and forget that love is about understanding—not about winning. It’s so easy to think that if someone agrees with us, we’ve connected. But true closeness? It comes from actually listening, from letting go of the need to have the last word. Sometimes, the bravest thing you can say is, “Tell me more,” or, “Help me understand.”
There’s a gentle wisdom in choosing curiosity over certainty. I heard a story once about a teacher who realized she learned far more from her students’ questions than from her own answers. When she stopped trying to be the expert, she created space for real learning—and for genuine connection. It’s amazing how much we miss when we’re just focused on proving our point.
Letting go doesn’t mean giving up what you believe in. It’s about holding your values with open hands—being willing to listen, to learn, and to grow. It’s choosing to value people over opinions, and connection over being right. When you do that, something shifts. Hearts soften, trust builds, and suddenly, there’s so much more room for love to grow.
